A content delivery network is a system of computers spread across many cities that store copies of websites so pages load quickly no matter where a visitor is located. Normally, every request for a webpage travels back to one main computer, called the origin server, which holds the original, complete version of the site. If that server sits far away, the trip takes noticeably longer. To fix this, copies of the site's files get placed on servers positioned closer to visitors, called edge locations, since they sit at the edge of the network, nearest to homes and offices rather than in one distant hub. When a request arrives and the nearby edge location already holds a stored copy, that success is called a cache hit, meaning the answer came back instantly without bothering the distant origin server at all. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries carrying copies of a popular book, so a reader nearby borrows one immediately instead of waiting for a package from a single faraway warehouse. This arrangement keeps websites fast, keeps them working even when traffic spikes, and reduces strain on the original source. Below is a short summary of the key terms involved.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|------|----------------|-----------------|
| Origin server | The main computer holding the real, original website files | Everything ultimately comes from here if no copy exists elsewhere |
| Edge location | A smaller server near everyday visitors, holding copies of site files | Shortens the distance data travels, speeding up loading |
| Cache hit | A moment when a nearby copy answers a request successfully | Avoids a slow trip to the origin server entirely |
| Content delivery network | The whole network of edge locations working together | Keeps busy websites fast and reliable worldwide |
